title: The questions left
tomorrow: Eli whispers he's not sure God exists. can he still read Torah?

cards: A kid asks the question you can't answer, and your face does the thing. Good question, you say, and change the subject. Not knowing can feel like failing the job.
But the Talmud sometimes fails the job on purpose. The rabbis argue a case back and forth, and the passage ends with one word: teiku. It stands.
Unresolved. Left on the page, and the discussion moves on. So does a teacher have to answer?
Two great voices in the tradition lean different ways.

teach.h: WHY RECORD THE OPINION THAT LOST?
teach.b: The first voice is the Talmud's own way, and the Mishnah says why. In the tractate Eduyot, it asks: why record the opinion that lost? And it answers: so that a later court can find it and rely on it someday.
The minority view is kept. The open question is kept. Its best case: the conversation is bigger than any one generation, and the next learner may see what you can't.

In the introduction to his great code, the Mishneh Torah, he says he gathered the law clearly, so that a person could read the Torah, then his book, and know what to do, without needing another book in between.
His best case: people have to live today. A family deciding how to keep Shabbat needs an answer, not a shelf of debates.
Here's what the tradition did with both. It kept the Talmud with its teiku. It kept Maimonides' code.
And later scholars printed their objections in the margins of his code, right next to his rulings. Answers and questions on the same page.

teach.h: WHAT WE DO, WHAT WE DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: So the honest teacher's move might be: here's what we do, and here's what we still don't know.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah keeps the losing argument on purpose, in case it's needed later.

how: Jewish learners study the Talmud with its open questions and minority views, and also turn to codes of law, such as Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, for what to do in practice.

practice: Write a short list of three questions you still carry about this path: one about a text, one about a practice, and one about meaning, or God, if that's yours. Don't answer them. Beside each one, write the word: stands.

wordCard.voice: The questions left: what every learner keeps after the lesson ends. The Talmud has a word for them, teiku, and it leaves them standing.

orig.note: Aramaic, in the Talmud: it stands. the word that leaves a question unresolved on the page.

carryVoice: Keep this one: questions left open; in the Talmud, teiku is a real ending too. Until tomorrow.
